"Rough call?" Lalit asked at the back door of the call centre, holding out a cigarette.
"No thanks." Zainab pressed both feet into the floor. "Give me a minute."
"What are you doing?"
"Feeling my feet. Now breathing out slower than I breathe in." She let out a long breath. "And naming things. Red fire door. Your blue lanyard. A crow on the wall."
"That works?"
"Better than scrolling for an hour till I feel nothing. I used to do that. Then the worry was still there, plus a lost hour."
"Huh."
"And when the worry started running my whole week, I began seeing a counsellor on Saturdays. This is one of the things we practised."
Lalit put the cigarette away. "Teach me the feet one?"

qa.a: Grounding brings her back to the present, while scrolling only numbed the worry and cost an hour; a counsellor helps once worry starts running the whole week.

qa.a: Lalit seems curious and open, putting the cigarette away and asking to learn the feet exercise.

passage:
A year ago I'd have got off the train. The carriage was packed, my chest went tight, and the old voice said, leave, leave now. Back then I left a lot. I skipped trips, cancelled dinners, and watched shows till two so I wouldn't have to feel anything. My brother Harish finally said, "Kashish, you've shrunk your whole life to your room." That stung, because it was true. That's when I found a counsellor.
So on the train last week, I did what we'd practised. Feet flat on the floor, feeling the shake of the tracks. A slow exhale, longer than the inhale. Then naming: yellow pole, a baby's sock, a man reading a newspaper. The tightness didn't vanish, but it shrank enough. I stayed on till Dadar. It's not magic. It's just something that helps instead of hides.

qa.q: Until which station did Kashish stay on the train?
qa.a: Kashish stayed on till Dadar.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when Harish said life had shrunk to one room?
qa.a: Kashish felt stung, because it was true, and that hurt led to finding a counsellor.

qa.q: Which grounding steps did Kashish use on the train, and why do they help?
qa.a: Feet flat on the floor, a slow long exhale and naming things nearby, which shrink the tightness enough to stay instead of escaping.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when speaking up?
qa.a: Harish was probably worried, watching Kashish skip trips and cancel dinners, and cared enough to say something hard.

grounding: A person replaces avoidance and numbing with grounding steps after seeking professional help because worry had shrunk their life.

Ward note, night shift
At 1 am Pema, our newest nurse, came out of bed 12 after a difficult conversation with a frightened family. I saw her go into the pantry and followed to check on her. She didn't reach for her phone, which I have seen her do before when upset, scrolling until break ended. Instead she stood with both feet planted, one hand on the counter, and breathed out slowly. Then, quietly, she named what she saw: 'Steel kettle. Blue mugs. Rain on the window.' After two minutes her colour came back. She told me that last month she had started seeing a counsellor, who taught her this. 'Scrolling made me feel nothing,' she said. 'This makes me feel here.' She finished her shift. I've suggested the whole team learn the steps at Friday's meeting.
Chinmay, ward in-charge

qa.q: What time did Pema come out of bed 12?
qa.a: At 1 am.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling when she came out of bed 12?
qa.a: She was shaken and upset after a hard conversation with a frightened family.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Pema, and why?
qa.a: Grounding by planting her feet, slowing her breath and naming what she saw, which kept her present instead of numbing out.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's view of Pema have changed after the pantry?
qa.a: Chinmay may now see her as someone learning healthy ways to cope, and useful to learn from, rather than just a new nurse.

grounding: Shows a young adult using grounding steps instead of numbing habits, with a counsellor's support, and an observer noting its effect.

passage:
Thursday
It happened on the metro again. Doors closed, the carriage packed, and my heart went off like an alarm. Old me would have got off at the next station, gone home and cancelled on Akash. I've cancelled on him three times this month. Today I tried the steps instead. Felt my feet in my sneakers, pressing down. Breathed out slowly, longer than in. Then named five things: a baby's yellow sock, a man's newspaper, the red line map, a scratch on the pole, my own hand. By the fourth stop my heart had slowed. I still felt shaky when I met Akash, but I was there. We ate momos and laughed. I'm writing this so I remember it works. And if this keeps ruling my days, I'll book the counsellor Akash mentioned. Disha

qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the metro doors closed?
qa.a: Disha felt a sudden rush of fear, heart going off like an alarm.

qa.a: Feeling feet in the sneakers, breathing out longer than in, and naming five things in the carriage.

qa.a: Akash may have been disappointed or worried, and glad that Disha showed up today.

passage: When the district inspector's jeep pulled up outside the village school, Nitin felt the old worry rise: tight throat, racing thoughts, the urge to hide in the storeroom with a bidi as he used to. Instead he stood by the window and pressed his feet into the floor. He breathed out slowly, longer than he breathed in. Then he named five things he could see: the neem tree, a goat, Class 3's paper boats, the chalk dust, Seema Madam's red umbrella. His shoulders dropped. He went out to greet the inspector. That evening he told his wife he was still having these waves most days, and that he would see the counsellor at the district hospital next week.

qa.a: The neem tree, a goat, Class 3's paper boats, the chalk dust and Seema Madam's red umbrella.

qa.a: Pressing his feet into the floor, a long slow out-breath and naming five things he could see, plus planning to see a counsellor since the waves continue.

qa.a: The worry would have been numbed for a moment but not eased, and he would have missed greeting the inspector.
